name: OneTab
tagline: One click collapses every open tab into a list — free, no account

pricing.notes: The core tab-saving extension is free. Current official help documents optional encrypted cloud backup and sync; this check did not establish its current license price. Core price record retains its August 2 verification.

pros: Free local tab saving; optional encrypted cloud backup and sync is a separate service with its own license terms
One-click tab collapse that the developer says cuts browser memory use by up to 95%
Local saved tabs stay in your browser; optional cloud backup encrypts them, and sharing a list publishes its links
Actively developed again — a 2026 v2 rewrite added folders, search, stars, tasks, and dark mode
Share-as-web-page turns any tab list into an instant public URL for another person or device
Plain-text export and a 2M+ Chrome install base mean lock-in is close to zero
cons: Real data-loss risk: uninstalling the extension deletes your stored tabs, and clearing browser data can wipe them too
Saves URLs and titles only — no page content, snapshots, or full-text search, so a dead link means the content is gone
No mobile story at all: no iOS or Android app and no web app to view your list from a phone
The Mac-only Safari app is a minimal port stuck well behind the Chrome version
Optional cloud backup and sync is distinct from local tab saving; check current license terms before enabling it.
bestFor: People who want to park open tabs as organized URL lists; check optional sync separately if you need access across computers.
verdict: The best free tab parker ever made; just don't mistake a local URL list for a permanent library.
overview: OneTab is a browser extension that stores open tabs as grouped URL lists and restores them individually or together. Current official help describes folders, saved-tab search, stars and tasks, and optional encrypted cloud backup and synchronization. Local tab saving and sharing a group as a public webpage are distinct from the optional sync service. It stores links rather than full article archives. Back up saved lists before uninstalling: its help warns that uninstalling deletes the browser’s stored tabs.

faqs.a: The core tab-saving extension is free. Optional backup and sync is now documented; check the current service terms and license price separately. The older coming-soon description is outdated.

Yes — and more actively than its reputation suggests. After years of near-silence that earned it an 'abandoned' label, OneTab shipped a full v2 rewrite in 2026 with folders, search, stars, tasks, and dark mode; the Chrome and Firefox extensions were both updated in July 2026. The weak spot is the Mac Safari app, which hasn't been updated since late 2024.

faqs.q: What is the best OneTab alternative?
faqs.a: Choose Workona or Toby for a different tab-workspace workflow. If you want to keep links as a reference library, Marqly saves open tabs with keyword search on its free plan of up to 100 saves; Pro adds automatic tags, summaries, and semantic search. OneTab also documents optional cloud sync, so compare that service separately.

OneTab does not provide an iOS or Android app. It documents sharing tab groups as webpages, which you can open on a phone. Optional encrypted backup and sync is a separate service; check its device support before relying on it for mobile access.

faqs.q: Can I export my data from OneTab?
faqs.a: Yes, easily. OneTab exports your saved tabs as a plain-text list of URLs with page titles, one per line, which you can copy anywhere and re-import into OneTab on another machine. You can also share any list as a hosted web page. There's no HTML, JSON, or CSV format, but a text list of URLs is about as portable as data gets.
